1	import MIPStarRE.LDT.Basic.ParametersBase
     2	
     3	/-!
     4	# Axis-parallel lines for the low individual degree test
     5	
     6	Axis-parallel line geometry on top of the core parameter infrastructure:
     7	`AxisParallelLine` records a base point and a coordinate direction, with
     8	canonical parameterization, rebasing, and slice-embedding operations.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	- `references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex`
    13	- `blueprint/src/chapter/ch02_test.tex`
    14	-/
    15	
    16	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    17	
    18	/-- A genuinely axis-parallel affine line in `F_q^m`. -/
    19	structure AxisParallelLine (params : Parameters) where
    20	  base : Point params
    21	  direction : Fin params.m
    22	
    23	deriving instance DecidableEq, Inhabited for AxisParallelLine
    24	
    25	namespace AxisParallelLine
    26	
    27	/-- The canonical affine parameterization `t ↦ base + t e_i`. -/
    28	def pointAt {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    29	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) : Fq params → Point params :=
    30	  fun t i =>
    31	    if i = ℓ.direction then
    32	      addCoord (ℓ.base i) t
    33	    else
    34	      ℓ.base i
    35	
    36	/-- Canonical geometric axis-parallel line through `u` in direction `i`.
    37	
    38	The representative stores zero in the moving coordinate, so all points on the
    39	same geometric line map to the same `AxisParallelLine`. -/
    40	def throughPoint {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    41	    (u : Point params) (i : Fin params.m) : AxisParallelLine params where
    42	  base := fun j => if j = i then zeroCoord else u j
    43	  direction := i
    44	
    45	/-- Affine parameter of the sampled point on the canonical axis-parallel line
    46	through `u` in direction `i`. -/
    47	def sampleParameter {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    48	    (u : Point params) (i : Fin params.m) : Fq params :=
    49	  u i
    50	
    51	/-- Rebase an axis-parallel line so that the old point `ℓ.pointAt t`
    52	becomes the new base point. -/
    53	def rebaseAt {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    54	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) (t : Fq params) : AxisParallelLine params where
    55	  base := ℓ.pointAt t
    56	  direction := ℓ.direction
    57	
    58	@[simp] theorem rebaseAt_pointAt_zero {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    59	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) (t : Fq params) :
    60	    (rebaseAt ℓ t).pointAt zeroCoord = ℓ.pointAt t := by
    61	  ext i
    62	  simp [rebaseAt, pointAt, addCoord, zeroCoord]
    63	
    64	@[simp] theorem rebaseAt_zero {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    65	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) :
    66	    rebaseAt ℓ zeroCoord = ℓ := by
    67	  cases ℓ with
    68	  | mk base direction =>
    69	      change
    70	        ({ base :=
    71	             ({ base := base, direction := direction } : AxisParallelLine params).pointAt zeroCoord,
    72	           direction := direction } : AxisParallelLine params) =
    73	        ({ base := base, direction := direction } : AxisParallelLine params)
    74	      congr
    75	      funext i
    76	      simp [pointAt, addCoord, zeroCoord]
    77	
    78	@[simp] theorem rebaseAt_direction {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    79	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) (t : Fq params) :
    80	    (rebaseAt ℓ t).direction = ℓ.direction :=
    81	  rfl
    82	
    83	/-- The canonical affine parameterization of `throughPoint u i` at parameter
    84	`sampleParameter u i = u i` returns the original point `u`. -/
    85	@[simp] theorem throughPoint_pointAt_sampleParameter {params : Parameters}
    86	    [FieldModel params.q] (u : Point params) (i : Fin params.m) :
    87	    (throughPoint (params := params) u i).pointAt
    88	        (sampleParameter (params := params) u i) = u := by
    89	  ext j
    90	  by_cases h : j = i
    91	  · subst h
    92	    simp [throughPoint, pointAt, sampleParameter, addCoord, zeroCoord]
    93	  · simp [throughPoint, pointAt, h]
    94	
    95	/-- Rebasing the canonical line `throughPoint u i` at its sample parameter yields
    96	the axis-parallel line with base `u` and direction `i`. -/
    97	@[simp] theorem rebaseAt_throughPoint_sampleParameter {params : Parameters}
    98	    [FieldModel params.q] (u : Point params) (i : Fin params.m) :
    99	    rebaseAt (throughPoint (params := params) u i)
   100	        (sampleParameter (params := params) u i) =
   101	      { base := u, direction := i } := by
   102	  change
   103	    ({ base :=
   104	        (throughPoint (params := params) u i).pointAt
   105	          (sampleParameter (params := params) u i)
   106	       direction := i } : AxisParallelLine params) =
   107	      { base := u, direction := i }
   108	  congr
   109	  exact throughPoint_pointAt_sampleParameter u i
   110	
   111	/-- Embed an axis-parallel line into the slice at height `x`. -/
   112	def appendAtHeight (params : Parameters)
   113	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) (x : Fq params) : AxisParallelLine params.next where
   114	  base := appendPoint params ℓ.base x
   115	  direction := embedCoord params ℓ.direction
   116	
   117	@[simp] theorem appendAtHeight_rebaseAt {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   118	    (ℓ : AxisParallelLine params) (t x : Fq params) :
   119	    appendAtHeight params (rebaseAt ℓ t) x =
   120	      rebaseAt (appendAtHeight params ℓ x) t := by
   121	  cases ℓ with
   122	  | mk base direction =>
   123	      change
   124	        ({ base :=
   125	             appendPoint params
   126	               (({ base := base, direction := direction } : AxisParallelLine params).pointAt t) x,
   127	           direction := embedCoord params direction } : AxisParallelLine params.next) =
   128	        ({ base :=
   129	             ({ base := appendPoint params base x,
   130	                direction := embedCoord params direction } :
   131	                AxisParallelLine params.next).pointAt t,
   132	           direction := embedCoord params direction } : AxisParallelLine params.next)
   133	      congr
   134	      funext i
   135	      by_cases hdir : i = embedCoord params direction
   136	      · subst i
   137	        simp [appendPoint, pointAt, embedCoord]
   138	        rfl
   139	      · by_cases hi : i.1 < params.m
   140	        · have hdir' : (⟨i.1, hi⟩ : Fin params.m) ≠ direction := by
   141	            intro h
   142	            apply hdir
   143	            apply Fin.ext
   144	            simpa [embedCoord] using congrArg Fin.val h
   145	          simp [appendPoint, pointAt, hi, hdir, hdir']
   146	        · simp [appendPoint, pointAt, hi, hdir]
   147	
   148	end AxisParallelLine
   149	
   150	end MIPStarRE.LDT

item.text: The geometry proofs themselves are grounded and remove the five tracked `sorry` sites cleanly. The more serious question is the strategy adapter: the direct game exposes a sampled diagonal index, while the mature LDT line measurement is indexed only by the line. I’m checking whether the implementation actually removes that extra information or merely selects one direct index.

280	\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}
   281	and the tensor-code test is likewise a test about the code
   282	$\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$, not about an encoding of indices into $\F_q$.  The
   283	$\chi$-based packaging exists so that the question distribution is
   284	conditionally linear, which the introspection machinery requires for the
   285	game the players actually play --- the Pauli basis test at dimension $m$,
   286	where admissibility does supply the divisibility.  The game at dimension
   287	$2m+2$ never appears in a verifier; it is an internal analysis device in the
   288	proof of the polynomial-pair lemma, so nothing there requires its question
   289	distribution to be conditionally linear.
   290	
   291	\section{Candidate repairs}
   292	
   293	\paragraph{Direct index sampling (candidate direction, recommended).}
   294	Define, for arbitrary $m' \ge 1$, the line-point distribution over
   295	$\F_q^{m'}$ that samples the uniform point, the uniform axis index
   296	$i \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$, and the diagonal direction with vanishing first
   297	$i-1$ coordinates, directly; define the \emph{directly indexed game} with
   298	this question distribution, whose line questions carry the index $i$ (and,
   299	for diagonal lines, the projected direction) in place of the seed
   300	$s \in \F_q$; and state the imported soundness theorem for that game
   301	(form~4 above).  This removes the divisibility obstruction and nothing
   302	else: the directly indexed game still asks for polynomials on revealed
   303	lines, has no pair questions, and weighs its branches as the present game
   304	does, so establishing form~4 carries the same two import obligations as
   305	the $\chi$-based import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), now at
   306	arbitrary dimension.
   307	
   308	The relation to the present game when $m' \mid q$ must moreover be proved
   309	at the level of games, not merely of question distributions, because the
   310	two games have different question alphabets: an $\mathsf{ALine}$ question
   311	of the $\chi$-based game is a pair $(u_0, s)$ and a $\mathsf{DLine}$
   312	question a triple $(u_0, s, v')$, so a strategy may select different
   313	measurements for seeds $s \ne s'$ with $\chi(s) = \chi(s')$, and equality
   314	of the induced laws of the geometric data does not by itself transport
   315	such a strategy.  The transport layer decomposes into the following
   316	obligations, none of which is carried out here.
   317	\begin{itemize}
   318	  \item \emph{Distribution lemma.}  When $m' \mid q$, the image of the
   319	  conditionally linear question distribution under the parsing map
   320	  $(u_0,s) \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s))$, $(u_0,s,v') \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s),v')$
   321	  is the direct distribution, and conditioned on the parsed question the
   322	  seed is uniform on the class $\chi^{-1}(i)$, independently of everything
   323	  else.
   324	  \item \emph{Parsing pullback.}  A strategy for the directly indexed game
   325	  composed with the parsing map is a seed-oblivious strategy for the
   326	  $\chi$-based game.  Since the win predicate depends on the question only
   327	  through the parsed data, and a seed-oblivious strategy answers
   328	  identically across each fiber --- in particular on the synchronicity
   329	  branches, where both players hold the same seed --- the value should be
   330	  preserved exactly on every branch, and projectivity is preserved.  This
   331	  is the direction the combining subtree needs.
   332	  \item \emph{Seed-fiber averaging: what it preserves and what it does
   333	  not.}  In the opposite direction, average each line measurement over its
   334	  seed fiber: attach to a direct question $(u_0,i)$, respectively
   335	  $(u_0,i,v')$, the average over uniform $s \in \chi^{-1}(i)$ of the
   336	  measurements attached to $(u_0,s)$, respectively $(u_0,s,v')$, leaving
   337	  the points measurements unchanged.  By the conditional uniformity of the
   338	  seed this preserves the value of every \emph{line-versus-point} branch
   339	  exactly: there the paired question carries no seed, so the branch value
   340	  is an average over the fiber of per-seed values, which the averaged
   341	  measurement computes.  It does \emph{not} preserve the synchronicity
   342	  branches.  There both players hold the same seed, so the $\chi$-based
   343	  branch value is the diagonal average
   344	  $\E_{s}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s)}_f
   345	  \rangle$, while the averaged strategy realizes the double average
   346	  $\E_{s,s'}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s')}_f
   347	  \rangle$ over independent seeds in the fiber; the two differ whenever
   348	  the players' measurements vary across a fiber in a correlated way (if
   349	  both apply a common seed-dependent relabelling, every diagonal term is
   350	  large and the cross terms are not), and neither quantity dominates the
   351	  other in general.  An earlier revision of this note claimed that the
   352	  averaging preserves the exact value, and with it synchronicity; that
   353	  claim was wrong and is withdrawn.  What needs proof is control of the
   354	  synchronicity branches under de-seeding.  Candidate approaches: show
   355	  that a strategy of value $1-\eps$ in the $\chi$-based game is, with
   356	  polynomial loss, close to a seed-oblivious one; or state form~4 with a
   357	  synchronicity hypothesis in the doubled-average form and re-derive it on
   358	  the tensor-code side.  Choosing and proving one of these is an open
   359	  obligation.
   360	  \item \emph{Projectivity round trip.}  The averaged strategy is a POVM
   361	  strategy even when the given one is projective, while the imported
   362	  theorem, like the present one, takes projective strategies.  The
   363	  intended round trip is: dilate the averaged strategy to a projective one
   364	  (Naimark preserves all product correlations
   365	  $\langle X \ot Y \rangle$ of the given strategy against the dilated
   366	  state --- hence the value of every branch the averaging preserved ---
   367	  but nothing restores the diagonal seed correlations once the averaging
   368	  has been performed); apply form~4; and compress the resulting polynomial
   369	  measurement along the dilation isometry back to a POVM in the required
   370	  measurement class on the original space.  That this compression
   371	  preserves the consistency conclusions must itself be proved; it is
   372	  stated here as an obligation, not established.  (Alternatively, form~4
   373	  may be stated for POVM strategies outright, moving the dilation inside
   374	  the import.)
   375	\end{itemize}
   376	
   377	The combining subtree would then be reread with the direct distribution

   442	\section{Conclusion}
   443	
   444	There is a theorem-level gap in the source proof route: the classical low
   445	individual degree game invoked at dimension $2m+2$ is undefined for every
   446	admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ (and for $(q,m) = (2,1)$), because its
   447	question distribution requires $2m+2 \mid q$ while admissibility supplies
   448	only $m \mid q$.  The cited route therefore does not establish the
   449	polynomial-pair lemma, nor the soundness of the Pauli basis test that
   450	depends on it, beyond $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.  Independently of the
   451	divisibility, the import of the classical game's quantum soundness carries
   452	the two open verification obligations of
   453	Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}: the asserted identity with the
   454	two-prover tensor-code test must be replaced by a reduction carrying a
   455	value bound, and the source's instantiation of the auxiliary parameter
   456	violates the theorem's lower bound at the small dimensions listed there.
   457	We do not assert that any conclusion is false: the underlying tensor-code
   458	soundness is insensitive to how the axis index is sampled, and both import
   459	obligations concern verification, not counterexample.  For the divisibility
   460	repair, the recommended candidate direction is direct index sampling ---
   461	restate the imported soundness theorem for the directly indexed game at
   462	arbitrary dimension; prove the distribution and parsing-pullback lemmas;
   463	settle the synchronicity control for de-seeding together with the
   464	dilation--compression round trip, so that the present soundness statement
   465	would follow from the repaired import; and reread the combining subtree
   466	against the directly indexed game --- a direction whose open obligations
   467	are enumerated under the candidate repairs, not an established route, with
   468	dimension padding as the fallback confined to the present game definition.

   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.

   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}
   449	\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
   450	\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
   451	\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
   452	\end{enumerate}
   453	
   454	As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   455	
   456	To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
   457	via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
   458	\end{proof}

    22	/-- A finite-support weighted distribution with nonnegative real-valued weights. -/
    23	structure Distribution (α : Type*) where
    24	  support : Finset α := ∅
    25	  weight : α → Error := fun _ => 0
    26	  nonnegative : ∀ a, 0 ≤ weight a := by intro _; positivity
    27	  outsideSupport : ∀ a, a ∉ support → weight a = 0 := by intro _ _; rfl
    28	
    29	namespace Distribution
    30	
    31	/-- The total mass carried by the explicit support of a distribution. -/
    32	def totalWeight {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Error :=
    33	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a
    34	
    35	/-- A `Distribution` is probabilistic when its total mass is exactly `1`. -/
    36	def IsProbability {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Prop :=
    37	  𝒟.totalWeight = 1

    39	/-- Push a finite-support distribution forward along a map.
    40	
    41	This is the project `Distribution` analogue of `PMF.map`.  The support is the
    42	image of the original finite support, and each new weight is the sum of the
    43	weights in the corresponding fiber. -/
    44	noncomputable def map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    45	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) : Distribution β where
    46	  support := 𝒟.support.image e
    47	  weight := fun b => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a
    48	  nonnegative := fun _ => Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a
    49	  outsideSupport := fun _ hb =>
    50	    Finset.sum_eq_zero fun a ha =>
    51	      (hb (Finset.mem_image.mpr
    52	        ⟨a, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).1, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2⟩)).elim
    53	
    54	@[simp]
    55	theorem map_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    56	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    57	    (𝒟.map e).support = 𝒟.support.image e := rfl
    58	
    59	@[simp]
    60	theorem map_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    61	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (b : β) :
    62	    (𝒟.map e).weight b =
    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by
    69	  simpa [totalWeight, map] using
    70	    (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    71	      (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)
    73	
    74	/-- A finite weighted sum over a push-forward distribution is the corresponding
    75	weighted sum of the pulled-back family.  This is the `Distribution` analogue of
    76	the finite-sum form of `PMF.map`. -/
    77	theorem map_sum_smul {α β M : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    78	    [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    79	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → M) :
    80	    ∑ b ∈ (𝒟.map e).support, (𝒟.map e).weight b • f b =
    81	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    82	  classical
    83	  calc
    84	    ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    85	        (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a) • f b
    86	        = ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    87	            ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    88	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    89	          intro b _
    90	          rw [Finset.sum_smul]
    91	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    92	          intro a ha
    93	          exact congrArg (fun x => 𝒟.weight a • f x) (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2.symm
    94	    _ = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    95	          exact Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    96	            (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    97	            (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩)
    98	            (fun a => 𝒟.weight a • f (e a))
    99

   102	/-- On a finite ambient type, a summand that vanishes outside a distribution's
   103	explicit support has the same total sum over all ambient values as over that support.
   104	
   105	This is a project-local explicit-support adapter around Mathlib's `Finset.sum_subset`:
   106	Mathlib supplies the finite-sum theorem, while this lemma packages the common shape used
   107	when paper expressions sum over a whole question set but the repository stores a smaller
   108	`Distribution.support`.  It is not intended to replace Mathlib probability theory. -/
   109	theorem Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support {α β : Type*} [Fintype α]
   110	    [AddCommMonoid β] (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → β)
   111	    (hf : ∀ a, a ∉ 𝒟.support → f a = 0) :
   112	    (∑ a : α, f a) = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, f a := by
   113	  classical
   114	  simpa using
   115	    (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   116	      (fun a _ ha => hf a ha)).symm

   120	/-- Unpack the equality form of the probability invariant. -/
   121	theorem weight_sum_eq_one {α : Type*}
   122	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   123	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   124	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.totalWeight] using h𝒟
   125	
   126	/-- A probability distribution has total weight one over any finite superset
   127	of its explicit support. -/
   128	theorem weight_sum_eq_one_of_subset {α : Type*}
   129	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) {s : Finset α}
   130	    (hsubset : 𝒟.support ⊆ s) :
   131	    ∑ a ∈ s, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   132	  have hsum :
   133	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = ∑ a ∈ s, 𝒟.weight a :=
   134	    Finset.sum_subset hsubset (fun a _ ha => 𝒟.outsideSupport a ha)
   135	  exact hsum ▸ h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one

   137	/-- On a finite ambient type, a probabilistic `Distribution` has total weight `1` even
   138	when its weights are summed over the whole ambient type.
   139	
   140	This packages the explicit-support bookkeeping in `Distribution` for downstream Lean
   141	statements that follow the paper's notation `𝔼_{x ∼ 𝒟}` over the question set rather
   142	than over a stored support finset. -/
   143	theorem weight_sum_univ_eq_one {α : Type*} [Fintype α]
   144	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   145	    (∑ a : α, 𝒟.weight a) = 1 := by
   146	  simpa using h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one_of_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   147	
   148	/-- A probability distribution has total weight at most `1`. -/
   149	theorem weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
   150	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   151	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1 :=
   152	  le_of_eq h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one

   154	/-- Push-forward preserves the probability invariant. -/
   155	theorem map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   156	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   157	    (𝒟.map e).IsProbability := by
   158	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.map_totalWeight] using h𝒟
   159

   164	/-- The Mathlib probability mass function associated to a project `Distribution`
   165	whose total mass is one.
   166	
   167	The construction sends each nonnegative real weight to `ℝ≥0∞` by
   168	`ENNReal.ofReal`; the hypotheses of `PMF.ofFinset` are exactly the project
   169	probability invariant and the stored zero-off-support condition. -/
   170	noncomputable def toPMF {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   171	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) : PMF α :=
   172	  PMF.ofFinset (fun a => ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a)) 𝒟.support
   173	    (by
   174	      rw [← ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a),
   175	        h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
   176	      simp)
   177	    (by
   178	      intro a ha
   179	      rw [𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   180	      simp)

   182	@[simp]
   183	theorem toPMF_apply {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   184	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   185	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a) := rfl

   187	@[simp]
   188	theorem toPMF_apply_toReal {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   189	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   190	    (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a).toReal = 𝒟.weight a := by
   191	  rw [toPMF_apply, ENNReal.toReal_ofReal (𝒟.nonnegative a)]

   193	/-- The associated PMF has zero mass outside the stored support of the project
   194	distribution. -/
   195	theorem toPMF_apply_of_notMem {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   196	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) {a : α} (ha : a ∉ 𝒟.support) :
   197	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = 0 := by
   198	  rw [toPMF_apply, 𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   199	  simp

   201	/-- The project push-forward agrees with Mathlib's push-forward of the
   202	associated probability mass function. -/
   203	theorem toPMF_map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   204	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   205	    (𝒟.map e).toPMF (h𝒟.map e) = (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟).map e := by
   206	  classical
   207	  ext b
   208	  rw [toPMF_apply, PMF.map_apply, map_weight]
   209	  rw [ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg
   210	    (s := 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b))
   211	    (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a)]
   212	  rw [tsum_eq_sum (s := 𝒟.support)]
   213	  · rw [Finset.sum_filter]
   214	    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
   215	    intro a ha
   216	    by_cases hea : e a = b
   217	    · have hba : b = e a := hea.symm
   218	      rw [if_pos hea, if_pos hba, toPMF_apply]
   219	    · have hba : b ≠ e a := fun hba => hea hba.symm
   220	      rw [if_neg hea, if_neg hba]
   221	  · intro a ha
   222	    by_cases hba : b = e a
   223	    · rw [if_pos hba, toPMF_apply_of_notMem 𝒟 h𝒟 ha]
   224	    · rw [if_neg hba]
   225	
   226	end Distribution

   229	def avgOver {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → Error) : Error :=
   230	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a * f a

   234	/-- The module-valued weighted finite sum associated to a finite-support `Distribution`,
   235	as a linear map in the averaged family.
   236	
   237	This packages the finite-support expression underlying both scalar averages and
   238	operator averages.  It keeps the explicit support carried by `Distribution`,
   239	while exposing the `Error`-module structure of the weighted sum. -/
   240	noncomputable def weightedSumLinearMap (M : Type*) [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
   241	    {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : (α → M) →ₗ[Error] M where
   242	  toFun := fun f => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a
   243	  map_add' := fun f g => by
   244	    simp only [Pi.add_apply, smul_add, Finset.sum_add_distrib]
   245	  map_smul' := fun c f => by
   246	    simp only [Pi.smul_apply]
   247	    calc
   248	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • c • f a =
   249	          ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, c • (𝒟.weight a • f a) := by
   250	            refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
   251	            intro a _
   252	            rw [smul_smul, smul_smul, mul_comm]
   253	      _ = c • ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a := by
   254	            rw [Finset.smul_sum]
   255

   257	theorem weightedSumLinearMap_apply (M : Type*) [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
   258	    {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → M) :
   259	    𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap M f = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a :=
   260	  rfl

   266	    avgOver 𝒟 f = 𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap Error f := by

   269	/-- Averaging against a pushed-forward distribution is averaging the pulled-back
   270	function against the original distribution. -/

   272	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → Error) :
   273	    avgOver (𝒟.map e) f = avgOver 𝒟 (fun a => f (e a)) := by

   414	/-- The uniform distribution on a specified finite support.
   415	
   416	The stored support is `s`, and the weight of a point is the elementary finite
   417	uniform weight `1 / s.card` on `s` and `0` off `s`.  When the support is empty
   418	this gives the zero sub-probability distribution, matching the convention used
   419	for degenerate filtered supports in the LDT development. -/
   420	noncomputable def uniformOnFinset {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) : Distribution α :=
   421	  letI := Classical.decEq α
   422	  { support := s
   423	    weight := fun a => if a ∈ s then 1 / (s.card : Error) else 0
   424	    nonnegative := fun _ => by
   425	      split_ifs <;> positivity
   426	    outsideSupport := fun _ ha => by
   427	      simp [ha] }
   428	
   429	@[simp]
   430	theorem uniformOnFinset_support {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) :
   431	    (uniformOnFinset s).support = s := rfl
   432	
   433	@[simp]
   434	theorem uniformOnFinset_weight {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (s : Finset α) (a : α) :
   435	    (uniformOnFinset s).weight a =
   436	      if a ∈ s then 1 / (s.card : Error) else 0 := by
   437	  by_cases ha : a ∈ s
   438	  · simp [uniformOnFinset, ha]
   439	  · simp [uniformOnFinset, ha]
   440	
   441	/-- A nonempty finite support gives a probability distribution. -/
   442	theorem uniformOnFinset_isProbability {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty) :
   443	    (uniformOnFinset s).IsProbability := by
   444	  classical
   445	  dsimp [IsProbability, totalWeight]
   446	  simp_rw [uniformOnFinset_weight]
   447	  have hcard_nat : s.card ≠ 0 := Finset.card_ne_zero.mpr hs
   448	  have hcard : (s.card : Error) ≠ 0 := by
   449	    exact_mod_cast hcard_nat
   450	  have hsum :
   451	      (∑ a ∈ s, if a ∈ s then 1 / (s.card : Error) else 0) =
   452	        ∑ _a ∈ s, 1 / (s.card : Error) := by
   453	    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
   454	    intro a ha
   455	    simp [ha]
   456	  rw [hsum]
   457	  simp [Finset.sum_const, hcard]
   458	
   459	/-- The uniform distribution on any finite support is a sub-probability
   460	distribution.  It has mass `1` on nonempty support and mass `0` on empty
   461	support. -/
   462	theorem uniformOnFinset_weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) :
   463	    ∑ a ∈ (uniformOnFinset s).support, (uniformOnFinset s).weight a ≤ 1 := by
   464	  classical
   465	  by_cases hs : s.Nonempty
   466	  · exact (uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs).weight_sum_le_one
   467	  · have hsempty : s = ∅ := Finset.not_nonempty_iff_eq_empty.mp hs
   468	    simp [hsempty]

import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Combining.DirectLowDegree.Soundness

/-!
# The directly indexed low-degree game

The low-degree game used by the Pauli-basis combining argument is needed in
dimension `2 * m + 2`.  The existing conditionally linear game represents a
coordinate index by an equally sized fiber in the scalar field and therefore
requires the dimension to divide the field size.  This file gives the separate
directly indexed variant which samples that index directly.

The geometric line carrier records the sampled coordinate, and line evaluation
uses an `Option` outcome rather than assigning a value when a point does not
determine one.  The game retains the point, axis-line, and diagonal-line answer
formats and the nine ordered type branches of the original low-degree game.

## References

The underlying game is `def:ld-game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with source origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
The need for the directly indexed repair in Chapter 15 is explained around
`rem:qld-4-7-divisibility` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:1257-1293` and in
`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`.
-/

   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

    71	An important class of strategies are those which are \emph{symmetric}.
    72	In this case, the bipartite state $\ket{\psi}$ Alice and Bob share is symmetric.
    73	Furthermore, for any question Alice and Bob receive, they apply the same measurement to their share of the state.
    74	This means that rather than, for example, keeping track of a separate points measurement for Alice and Bob,
    75	we can use a single measurement to refer to both of their strategies,
    76	and similarly for the axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines measurements.
    77	This is formalized in the following definition, where we also consider strategies which are projective.
    78	
    79	\begin{definition}[Symmetric, projective strategy]
    80	A \emph{symmetric, projective strategy} for the $(m,q, d)$-low individual degree test
    81	is a tuple $(\psi, A, B, L)$ defined as follows.
    82	\begin{itemize}
    83	\item[$\circ$] $\ket{\psi} \in \calH \ot \calH$ is a bipartite, permutation-invariant state.
    84	\item[$\circ$] $A = \{A^u_a\}$ contains a matrix for each $u \in \F_q^m$ and $a \in \F_q$.
    85				For each $u$, $A^u$ is a projective measurement on~$\calH$.
    86	\item[$\circ$] $B = \{B^{\ell}_f\}$ contains a matrix for each axis-parallel line~$\ell$ in $\F_q^m$
    87				and univariate degree-$d$ polynomial $f:\ell\rightarrow \F_q$.
    88				For each $\ell$, $B^{\ell}$ is a projective measurement on~$\calH$.
    89	\item[$\circ$] $L = \{L^{\ell}_f\}$ contains a matrix for each line~$\ell$ in $\F_q^m$
    90				and univariate degree-$md$ polynomial $f:\ell\rightarrow \F_q$.
    91				For each $\ell$, $L^{\ell}$ is a projective measurement on~$\calH$.
    92	\end{itemize}
    93	\end{definition}
    94	
    95	We can also consider more general strategies which are no longer assumed to be symmetric.
    96	In this case, Players~$\mathrm{A}$ and~$\mathrm{B}$ each have their own versions of the measurements~$A$, $B$, and~$L$.
    97	
    98	\begin{definition}[General projective strategy]
    99	A \emph{projective strategy} for the $(m,q, d)$-low individual degree test
   100	is a tuple $(\psi, A^{\mathrm{A}},B^{\mathrm{A}},L^{\mathrm{A}},A^{\mathrm{B}},B^{\mathrm{B}},L^{\mathrm{B}})$ defined as follows.
   101	\begin{itemize}
   102	\item[$\circ$] $\ket{\psi} \in \calH_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \calH_{\mathrm{B}}$ is a bipartite state.
   103	\end{itemize}
   104	Furthermore, for each~$w \in \{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}\}$:
   105	\begin{itemize}
   106	\item[$\circ$] $A^{w} = \{A^{w,u}_a\}$ contains a matrix for each $u \in \F_q^m$ and $a \in \F_q$.
   107				For each $u$, $A^{w,u}$ is a projective measurement on~$\calH_{w}$.
   108	\item[$\circ$] $B^{w} = \{B^{w,\ell}_f\}$ contains a matrix for each axis-parallel line~$\ell$ in $\F_q^m$
   109				and univariate degree-$d$ polynomial $f:\ell\rightarrow \F_q$.
   110				For each $\ell$, $B^{w,\ell}$ is a projective measurement on~$\calH_{w}$.
   111	\item[$\circ$] $L^w = \{L^{w,\ell}_f\}$ contains a matrix for each line~$\ell$ in $\F_q^m$
   112				and univariate degree-$md$ polynomial $f:\ell\rightarrow \F_q$.
   113				For each $\ell$, $L^{w,\ell}$ is a projective measurement on~$\calH_{w}$.
   114	\end{itemize}
   115	\end{definition}
   116	
   117	\begin{remark}
   118	Throughout this work, we will only consider projective strategies.
   119	So we will henceforth use the terms ``strategy" and ``symmetric strategy'' to refer exclusively to projective strategies and symmetric, projective strategies, respectively.

   135	    (line : AxisParallelLine D.toLDTParameters)

   139	      ldtPointToDirect D line.base +

   146	    Pi.smul_apply]
   147	  by_cases hi : i = line.direction
   148	  · subst i
   149	    simp only [coordinateDirection, if_pos, smul_eq_mul]
   150	    rw [Pi.single_eq_same, mul_one]

   276	    {alpha beta gamma : Type*}

   280	    (e : alpha ≃ beta × gamma) (f : alpha → beta)
   281	    (hf : ∀ a, f a = (e a).1) :
   282	    (uniformDistribution alpha).map f = uniformDistribution beta := by
   283	  classical
   284	  have hsurjective : Function.Surjective f := by
   285	    intro b
   286	    let c : gamma := Classical.choice (inferInstance : Nonempty gamma)

/-- Quantum soundness obligation for the directly indexed low-degree game.
This is the repaired import form proposed in
`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`, needed by the Chapter 15
combining argument at paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1267-1288`.

This is a formalization auxiliary assertion, not the source-labelled
`lem:ld-soundness`.  Its proof must establish the game-correspondence and
auxiliary-parameter bounds catalogued in the cited gap note; neither is hidden
as a hypothesis here. -/
theorem exists_direct_ld_soundness :
    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b ≤ 1 ∧
      ∀ (D : DirectLdParams) (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
        ∀ S : Strategy (directLdGame D), S.IsProjective → 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
          ∃ GA : DirectPolyMeasTuple D S.ιA,
            ∃ GB : DirectPolyMeasTuple D S.ιB,
              consistencyDefect
                  (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
                  (fun u outcome =>
                    heteroKron
                      (((S.A (directLdPointQuestionOf D u)).postprocess
                        (directLdPointValuesOrZero D)).effect outcome) 1)
                  (fun u outcome =>
                    heteroKron 1
                      ((GB.postprocess (evalDirectPolyTupleAt u)).effect outcome))
                  S.ψ ≤ deltaLd a b ε D.q D.m D.d D.k ∧
              consistencyDefect
                  (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
                  (fun u outcome =>
                    heteroKron
                      ((GA.postprocess (evalDirectPolyTupleAt u)).effect outcome) 1)
                  (fun u outcome =>
                    heteroKron 1
                      (((S.B (directLdPointQuestionOf D u)).postprocess
                        (directLdPointValuesOrZero D)).effect outcome))
                  S.ψ ≤ deltaLd a b ε D.q D.m D.d D.k ∧
              consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Unit)
                  (fun _ g => heteroKron (GA.effect g) 1)
                  (fun _ g => heteroKron 1 (GB.effect g))
                  S.ψ ≤ deltaLd a b ε D.q D.m D.d D.k := by
  sorry

end

   291	\section{Candidate repairs}
   292	
   293	\paragraph{Direct index sampling (candidate direction, recommended).}
   294	Define, for arbitrary $m' \ge 1$, the line-point distribution over
   295	$\F_q^{m'}$ that samples the uniform point, the uniform axis index
   296	$i \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$, and the diagonal direction with vanishing first
   297	$i-1$ coordinates, directly; define the \emph{directly indexed game} with
   298	this question distribution, whose line questions carry the index $i$ (and,
   299	for diagonal lines, the projected direction) in place of the seed
   300	$s \in \F_q$; and state the imported soundness theorem for that game
   301	(form~4 above).  This removes the divisibility obstruction and nothing
   302	else: the directly indexed game still asks for polynomials on revealed
   303	lines, has no pair questions, and weighs its branches as the present game
   304	does, so establishing form~4 carries the same two import obligations as
   305	the $\chi$-based import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), now at
   306	arbitrary dimension.
   307	
   308	The relation to the present game when $m' \mid q$ must moreover be proved
   309	at the level of games, not merely of question distributions, because the
   310	two games have different question alphabets: an $\mathsf{ALine}$ question
   311	of the $\chi$-based game is a pair $(u_0, s)$ and a $\mathsf{DLine}$
   312	question a triple $(u_0, s, v')$, so a strategy may select different
   313	measurements for seeds $s \ne s'$ with $\chi(s) = \chi(s')$, and equality
   314	of the induced laws of the geometric data does not by itself transport
   315	such a strategy.  The transport layer decomposes into the following
   316	obligations, none of which is carried out here.
   317	\begin{itemize}
   318	  \item \emph{Distribution lemma.}  When $m' \mid q$, the image of the
   319	  conditionally linear question distribution under the parsing map
   320	  $(u_0,s) \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s))$, $(u_0,s,v') \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s),v')$
   321	  is the direct distribution, and conditioned on the parsed question the
   322	  seed is uniform on the class $\chi^{-1}(i)$, independently of everything
   323	  else.
   324	  \item \emph{Parsing pullback.}  A strategy for the directly indexed game
   325	  composed with the parsing map is a seed-oblivious strategy for the
   326	  $\chi$-based game.  Since the win predicate depends on the question only
   327	  through the parsed data, and a seed-oblivious strategy answers
   328	  identically across each fiber --- in particular on the synchronicity
   329	  branches, where both players hold the same seed --- the value should be
   330	  preserved exactly on every branch, and projectivity is preserved.  This
   331	  is the direction the combining subtree needs.
   332	  \item \emph{Seed-fiber averaging: what it preserves and what it does
   333	  not.}  In the opposite direction, average each line measurement over its
   334	  seed fiber: attach to a direct question $(u_0,i)$, respectively
   335	  $(u_0,i,v')$, the average over uniform $s \in \chi^{-1}(i)$ of the
   336	  measurements attached to $(u_0,s)$, respectively $(u_0,s,v')$, leaving
   337	  the points measurements unchanged.  By the conditional uniformity of the
   338	  seed this preserves the value of every \emph{line-versus-point} branch
   339	  exactly: there the paired question carries no seed, so the branch value
   340	  is an average over the fiber of per-seed values, which the averaged
   341	  measurement computes.  It does \emph{not} preserve the synchronicity
   342	  branches.  There both players hold the same seed, so the $\chi$-based
   343	  branch value is the diagonal average
   344	  $\E_{s}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s)}_f
   345	  \rangle$, while the averaged strategy realizes the double average
   346	  $\E_{s,s'}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s')}_f
   347	  \rangle$ over independent seeds in the fiber; the two differ whenever
   348	  the players' measurements vary across a fiber in a correlated way (if
   349	  both apply a common seed-dependent relabelling, every diagonal term is
   350	  large and the cross terms are not), and neither quantity dominates the
   351	  other in general.  An earlier revision of this note claimed that the
   352	  averaging preserves the exact value, and with it synchronicity; that
   353	  claim was wrong and is withdrawn.  What needs proof is control of the
   354	  synchronicity branches under de-seeding.  Candidate approaches: show
   355	  that a strategy of value $1-\eps$ in the $\chi$-based game is, with
   356	  polynomial loss, close to a seed-oblivious one; or state form~4 with a
   357	  synchronicity hypothesis in the doubled-average form and re-derive it on
   358	  the tensor-code side.  Choosing and proving one of these is an open
   359	  obligation.

   361	  strategy even when the given one is projective, while the imported
   362	  theorem, like the present one, takes projective strategies.  The
   363	  intended round trip is: dilate the averaged strategy to a projective one
   364	  (Naimark preserves all product correlations
   365	  $\langle X \ot Y \rangle$ of the given strategy against the dilated
   366	  state --- hence the value of every branch the averaging preserved ---
   367	  but nothing restores the diagonal seed correlations once the averaging
   368	  has been performed); apply form~4; and compress the resulting polynomial
   369	  measurement along the dilation isometry back to a POVM in the required
   370	  measurement class on the original space.  That this compression
   371	  preserves the consistency conclusions must itself be proved; it is

    30	/-- A point differs from its canonical representative by a scalar multiple of
    31	the line direction. -/
    32	theorem mem_linePoints_direct_lineRepMap
    33	    {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ} (v u : Fin m → K) :
    34	    u ∈ linePoints (lineRepMap v u) v := by
    35	  let W : Submodule K (Fin m → K) := Submodule.span K ({v} : Set (Fin m → K))
    36	  let T : Submodule K (Fin m → K) :=
    37	    registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)
    38	  have hdiff : u - lineRepMap v u ∈ W := by
    39	    simpa [lineRepMap, canonicalProjOfKernel, W, T, LinearMap.comp_apply] using
    40	      (Submodule.sub_projection_mem
    41	        (isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement W).symm u)
    42	  rcases Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp hdiff with ⟨t, ht⟩
    43	  refine ⟨t, ?_⟩
    44	  rw [ht]
    45	  abel
    46	
    47	/-- A chosen affine parameter expressing a point relative to its canonical
    48	line representative. -/
    49	noncomputable def directLineRepParameter
    50	    {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ} (v u : Fin m → K) : K :=
    51	  Classical.choose (mem_linePoints_direct_lineRepMap v u)
    52	
    53	/-- The chosen canonical rebase parameter reconstructs the original point. -/
    54	theorem directLineRepParameter_spec
    55	    {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ} (v u : Fin m → K) :
    56	    u = lineRepMap v u + directLineRepParameter v u • v :=
    57	  Classical.choose_spec (mem_linePoints_direct_lineRepMap v u)
    58	
    59	/-- Canonical line representatives are unchanged by translation along their
    60	direction. -/
    61	theorem lineRepMap_add_smul
    62	    {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    63	    (v u : Fin m → K) (t : K) :
    64	    lineRepMap v (u + t • v) = lineRepMap v u := by
    65	  let W : Submodule K (Fin m → K) := Submodule.span K ({v} : Set (Fin m → K))
    66	  have hv : v ∈ W := Submodule.subset_span (Set.mem_singleton v)
    67	  have hzero : lineRepMap v v = 0 := by
    68	    simp [lineRepMap, canonicalProjOfKernel, W, LinearMap.comp_apply,
    69	      Submodule.projectionOnto_apply_of_mem_right
    70	        (isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement W).symm hv]
    71	  simp [map_add, map_smul, hzero]
    72	
    73	/-- For a nonzero direction, the canonical rebase parameter is unique. -/
    74	theorem directLineRepParameter_eq_of_nonzero
    75	    {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    76	    {v u : Fin m → K} (hv : v ≠ 0) {t : K}
    77	    (ht : u = lineRepMap v u + t • v) :
    78	    directLineRepParameter v u = t := by
    79	  have hfun : directLineRepParameter v u • v = t • v := by
    80	    apply add_left_cancel (a := lineRepMap v u)
    81	    exact (directLineRepParameter_spec v u).symm.trans ht
    82	  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ : ∃ i, v i ≠ 0 := by
    83	    by_contra h
    84	    apply hv
    85	    funext i
    86	    simpa using not_exists.mp h i
    87	  have hcoord := congrFun hfun i
    88	  simp only [Pi.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul] at hcoord
    89	  exact mul_right_cancel₀ hi hcoord
    90	
    91	/-- Translating a point on a nonzero line adds the translation to its
    92	canonical rebase parameter. -/
    93	theorem directLineRepParameter_add_smul
    94	    {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    95	    {v u : Fin m → K} (hv : v ≠ 0) (t : K) :
    96	    directLineRepParameter v (u + t • v) =
    97	      directLineRepParameter v u + t := by
    98	  apply directLineRepParameter_eq_of_nonzero hv
    99	  rw [lineRepMap_add_smul]
   100	  calc
   101	    u + t • v =
   102	        (lineRepMap v u + directLineRepParameter v u • v) + t • v := by
   103	      rw [← directLineRepParameter_spec v u]
   104	    _ = lineRepMap v u + (directLineRepParameter v u + t) • v := by
   105	      module

   108	abbrev ldtPointToDirect (D : DirectLdParams) :
   109	    Point D.toLDTParameters → Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D :=
   110	  (directPointEquiv D).symm

item.text: The source comparison confirms the fixed-index issue is not cosmetic: the mature test samples a restriction index but only reveals the geometric line, while the direct game reveals the index. A transport theorem needs to preserve that averaging; selecting `firstIndex` for every line cannot do so. I’m checking the full new import chain now so the final review distinguishes semantic blockers from organization-only issues.

     4	/-!
     5	# Geometry for the directly indexed low-degree game
     6	
     7	This module defines the parameters, line carrier, and line-point distributions
     8	for the directly indexed low-degree game.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	The line-point distributions originate in
    13	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:243-272`.
    14	The directly indexed repair is documented in
    15	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`.
    16	-/
    17	
    18	open scoped BigOperators
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    21	
    22	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    23	open MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    24	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    25	
    26	noncomputable section
    27	
    28	/-- Parameters for the directly indexed low-degree game.  Unlike `LdParams`,
    29	this directly indexed line-space construction has no divisibility field: its coordinate index is
    30	sampled from `Fin m` rather than encoded by fibers of `chiIndex`.
    31	
    32	This is the direct-index repair described in
    33	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`; it is not a second
    34	definition of the source verifier game. -/
    35	structure DirectLdParams where
    36	  q : ℕ
    37	  m : ℕ
    38	  d : ℕ
    39	  k : ℕ
    40	  hm : 1 ≤ m
    41	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    42	  hk : 1 ≤ k
    43	  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
    44	
    45	/-- The canonical scalar model for directly indexed parameters. -/
    46	noncomputable def DirectLdParams.model (D : DirectLdParams) : FixedFieldModel D.q :=
    47	  fixedFieldModel D.q D.hq
    48	
    49	/-- The scalar field of a directly indexed low-degree game. -/
    50	abbrev DirectScalarQ (D : DirectLdParams) := D.model.K
    51	
    52	/-- The first coordinate, available because directly indexed dimensions are
    53	positive. -/
    54	def DirectLdParams.firstIndex (D : DirectLdParams) : Fin D.m :=

    16	/-- A genuinely affine diagonal line in `F_q^m`. -/
    17	structure DiagonalLine (params : Parameters) where

    19	  direction : Point params
    20	
    21	deriving instance DecidableEq, Inhabited for DiagonalLine
    22	
    23	namespace DiagonalLine

    25	/-- The canonical affine parameterization `t ↦ base + t · direction`. -/
    26	def pointAt {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    27	    (ℓ : DiagonalLine params) : Fq params → Point params :=
    28	  fun t => addPoint ℓ.base (smulPoint t ℓ.direction)
    29	
    30	/-- The support of the nonzero coordinates of a direction vector. -/
    31	noncomputable def nonzeroDirectionSupport {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    32	    (v : Point params) : Finset (Fin params.m) :=
    33	  Finset.univ.filter fun i => v i ≠ zeroCoord
    34	
    35	/-- The least nonzero coordinate of a direction vector, when one exists. -/
    36	noncomputable def firstNonzeroCoord? {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    37	    (v : Point params) : Option (Fin params.m) :=
    38	  open Classical in
    39	  let s := nonzeroDirectionSupport (params := params) v
    40	  if hs : s.Nonempty then some (s.min' hs) else none
    41	
    42	/-- Normalize a direction vector so its first nonzero coordinate becomes `1`. -/
    43	noncomputable def normalizeDirection {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    44	    (v : Point params) : Point params :=
    45	  open Classical in
    46	  match firstNonzeroCoord? (params := params) v with
    47	    | none => zeroPoint
    48	    | some i => smulPoint (invCoord (v i)) v
    49	
    50	/-- Canonical geometric diagonal line through `u` in direction `v`.
    51	
    52	For nonzero `v`, we normalize by the first nonzero coordinate and shift the
    53	base point so that this pivot coordinate is `0`. The degenerate `v = 0` case is
    54	kept as the singleton line through `u`. -/
    55	noncomputable def throughPointDirection {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    56	    (u v : Point params) : DiagonalLine params :=
    57	  open Classical in
    58	  match firstNonzeroCoord? (params := params) v with
    59	    | none => { base := u, direction := zeroPoint }
    60	    | some i =>
    61	        let w := normalizeDirection (params := params) v
    62	        let t := u i
    63	        { base := fun j => subCoord (u j) (mulCoord t (w j))
    64	          direction := w }

   195	structure DiagonalLinePolynomial (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q] where

   199	noncomputable instance {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] :

   204	namespace DiagonalLinePolynomial

   206	/-- Evaluation of a diagonal-line answer on the line parameter. -/
   207	noncomputable def toFun {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   208	    (f : DiagonalLinePolynomial params) : Fq params → Fq params :=

   211	noncomputable instance {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] :
   212	    CoeFun (DiagonalLinePolynomial params) (fun _ => Fq params → Fq params) :=
   213	  ⟨DiagonalLinePolynomial.toFun⟩

   215	@[ext] theorem ext {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   216	    {f g : DiagonalLinePolynomial params} (hpoly : f.poly = g.poly) : f = g := by
   217	  cases f with
   218	  | mk polyf hpolyf =>
   219	      cases g with
   220	      | mk polyg hpolyg =>
   221	          cases hpoly
   222	          congr

   224	/-- Reparametrize a diagonal-line answer by translating the line parameter.
   225	
   226	Concretely, the underlying univariate polynomial `f.poly` (over `Scalar params` in
   227	the chosen field model) is precomposed with `X + C (decodeScalar t)`, i.e. the
   228	coefficients are shifted using genuine *field* addition on `Scalar params` — not
   229	the `Fin q` arithmetic on `Fq params`. Transporting back through `encodeScalar`

   231	`reparamAt_apply`), where `addCoord` is field addition lifted through the coding
   232	`FieldModel.equiv`. Composition with a degree-one polynomial preserves the
   233	`natDegree ≤ params.m * params.d` bound.

   236	parameter `t`: the old parameter `addCoord t s` becomes the new parameter `s`. -/

   238	    (f : DiagonalLinePolynomial params) (t : Fq params) : DiagonalLinePolynomial params where

# MIPStarRE

This root module re-exports the finite-dimensional quantum infrastructure, the
low individual degree test formalization, and the quantum Pauli basis test
formalization used for the project surrounding the theorem \(MIP^* = RE\).

## References

- arXiv:2009.12982, *Low individual degree testing for quantum states*
- arXiv:2001.04383, *MIP*=RE*
- The active low individual degree test development in `MIPStarRE.LDT`

   400	Alternatively, embed the combined polynomial into

   414	One could instead define an index function at dimension $2m+2$ with classes

   422	
   423	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} keeps the sub-line lemma, the
   424	combined line lemma, and the polynomial-pair lemma in their source-shaped
   425	statements, with no divisibility hypothesis.  Their proofs retain the source
   426	constructions and mark the unresolved obligation at the exact steps: the
   427	first sampling step of the sub-line construction, where $\chi_{2m+2}$ and
   428	the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$ are invoked, and the
   429	instantiation step of the polynomial-pair proof, where $(q,2m+2,d,1)$ is
   430	used as a game parameter tuple.  A chapter remark records the divisibility
   431	arithmetic and cites this note; the final soundness theorem for the Pauli
   432	basis test remains open modulo this obligation.  The blueprint's proof node
   433	for the classical soundness import itself states the source's route --- the
   434	identification with the two-prover tensor-code test and the application of
   435	Theorem~4.7 --- and enumerates the two obligations of
   436	Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations} as open, citing this note for the
   437	detailed comparison and the case arithmetic.  An earlier revision had
   438	instead added the hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$ to the three lemmas; that was
   439	statement drift in the sense of the proof-gap protocol, since the hypothesis
   440	excludes all admissible $m \ge 2$ and does not appear in the source.

   442	\section{Conclusion}
   443	
   444	There is a theorem-level gap in the source proof route: the classical low
   445	individual degree game invoked at dimension $2m+2$ is undefined for every
   446	admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ (and for $(q,m) = (2,1)$), because its
   447	question distribution requires $2m+2 \mid q$ while admissibility supplies
   448	only $m \mid q$.  The cited route therefore does not establish the
   449	polynomial-pair lemma, nor the soundness of the Pauli basis test that
   450	depends on it, beyond $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.  Independently of the
   451	divisibility, the import of the classical game's quantum soundness carries
   452	the two open verification obligations of
   453	Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}: the asserted identity with the
   454	two-prover tensor-code test must be replaced by a reduction carrying a
   455	value bound, and the source's instantiation of the auxiliary parameter
   456	violates the theorem's lower bound at the small dimensions listed there.
   457	We do not assert that any conclusion is false: the underlying tensor-code
   458	soundness is insensitive to how the axis index is sampled, and both import
   459	obligations concern verification, not counterexample.  For the divisibility
   460	repair, the recommended candidate direction is direct index sampling ---
   461	restate the imported soundness theorem for the directly indexed game at
   462	arbitrary dimension; prove the distribution and parsing-pullback lemmas;
   463	settle the synchronicity control for de-seeding together with the
   464	dilation--compression round trip, so that the present soundness statement
   465	would follow from the repaired import; and reread the combining subtree
   466	against the directly indexed game --- a direction whose open obligations
   467	are enumerated under the candidate repairs, not an established route, with
   468	dimension padding as the fallback confined to the present game definition.

   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.

   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of

1	# Lean Proof-Evasion Anti-Patterns
     2	
     3	Catalog of subtle proof-evasion patterns that pass kernel-level checks
     4	(`sorry`-free, no forbidden tactics, all axioms standard) yet still fail to
     5	prove the claimed mathematics. Complements
     6	the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference, which covers the kernel-level
     7	blockers; this file covers patterns where the Lean code *compiles and the
     8	trick is at the level of what the statement says or what the definitions
     9	bake in*.
    10	
    11	Every pattern here is **castle-in-the-air in spirit**: a theorem named after a
    12	paper result that doesn't actually prove it. The named offenders below all
    13	cross-reference a concrete issue or PR so reviewers can see a real example.
    14	
    15	## Why this matters
    16	
    17	Kernel checks are necessary but not sufficient. A theorem can:
    18	
    19	- Be marked `\leanok` in the blueprint,
    20	- Have a sorry-free proof body,
    21	- Have a clean axiom closure (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` only),
    22	
    23	and still prove **nothing that the paper actually claims**, if the proof
    24	obligation has been displaced into a hypothesis, a definition, or a sentinel
    25	branch. The patterns below are the displacement mechanisms we've seen in this
    26	codebase.
    27	
    28	## Catalogue
    29	
    30	- [A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis](#a1--conclusion-shaped-hypothesis)
    31	- [A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand](#a2--definitional-sleight-of-hand)
    32	- [A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions](#a3--zero-fallback-branches-hiding-preconditions)
    33	- [A4 — Trivial default witnesses for existentials](#a4--trivial-default-witnesses-for-existentials)
    34	- [A5 — Castle-in-the-air / bypassing Mathlib](#a5--castle-in-the-air--bypassing-mathlib)
    35	- [A6 — External `*Statement` smuggles](#a6--external-statement-smuggles)
    36	
    37	---
    38	
    39	## A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis
    40	
    41	**Smell.** The theorem takes a hypothesis whose type is the theorem's own
    42	conclusion (or an `∃`/function that produces the conclusion). The proof body
    43	is a trivial `rcases`/`exact`/`.trans`/`simpa using h` and does no
    44	mathematical work. A variant wraps the hypothesis in a named bundle
    45	(`*BridgePackage`, `*Statement`); see issues [#449], [#451], [#477] for the
    46	catalogue, and [#493] for the inline-existential mutation triggered by
    47	PR [#491].
    48	
    49	### Why it's bad
    50	
    51	The theorem's named mathematical content is never derived from prior lemmas;
    52	the caller (who supplies the hypothesis) has to discharge it. In practice the
    53	caller then has the same problem, pushing the obligation further up the
    54	stack. The theorem is true under a vacuous hypothesis and the `\leanok` tag
    55	misrepresents the actual state of the proof.
    56	
    57	### How to spot it
    58	
    59	- The hypothesis type contains, up to `∃` / `∧` / a coercion, the theorem's
    60	  conclusion.
    61	- The proof body is one of:
    62	  - `rcases h with ⟨...⟩; exact ⟨...⟩`
    63	  - `exact h.fieldName` / `exact h.a.trans h.b`
    64	  - `by simpa using h.fieldName`
    65	- The hypothesis is a bundle named `*BridgePackage`, `*Witness`, `*Package`,
    66	  `*Output`, with a field whose type matches the conclusion structure.
    67	- Consumers of the bundle are trivial (field projection + return).
    68	
    69	### Concrete example
    70	
    71	Historical example (before the MainInductionStep cleanup):
    72	
    73	```lean
    74	theorem mainInduction
    75	    (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q]
    76	    (strategy : SymStrat params ι)
    77	    (eps delta gamma : Error) (k : ℕ)
    78	    (hbridge : MainInductionBridgePackage params strategy eps delta gamma k) :
    79	    ∃ G : Measurement (Polynomial params) ι,
    80	      ConsRel strategy.state ...
    81	        (mainInductionError params k eps delta gamma) := by
    82	  rcases hbridge.witness with ⟨error, G, hG, herror⟩
    83	  refine ⟨G, ?_⟩
    84	  exact ⟨le_trans hG.offDiagonalBound herror⟩
    85	```
    86	
    87	Here `MainInductionBridgePackage.witness` has type
    88	`∃ error, ∃ G, ConsRel ... error ∧ error ≤ mainInductionError ...` — literally
    89	the conclusion. The code has since been refactored to remove both this
    90	specific MainInductionStep bridge and the interim theorem alias that exposed
    91	the same witness shape under the paper theorem's name, but the snippet remains
    92	the archetypal example of the anti-pattern.
    93	
    94	PR [#491] proposed to delete the `*BridgePackage` by **inlining** the bundle's
    95	fields as explicit hypotheses. That only scatters the same pattern across
    96	individual signatures without producing any proof — it's strictly worse
    97	because the named bundle at least shows up in one tracker. Do not accept PRs
    98	that discharge an ungrounded bridge by flattening it into conclusion-shaped
    99	existential hypotheses, or by reintroducing the same shape under a theorem name
   100	that suggests the paper result has been proved.
   101	
   102	### How to fix it
   103	
   104	Prefer **proving a real intermediate lemma** — one that the paper also uses
   105	— and stating its signature with the paper's hypotheses (not the theorem's
   106	conclusion). Then use it inside the larger theorem. If the missing content
   107	cannot be formalized yet, state the missing assertion as a named obligation
   108	to be proved from the paper hypotheses, and leave the corresponding proof open
   109	under a tracker. Do not put that obligation on the source-labelled theorem as
   110	an extra hypothesis. Existing `BridgePackage`-style declarations are proof
   111	debt to be removed or converted into source-faithful obligations; they are not
   112	the preferred shape for new work.
   113	
   114	A signature passes the smell test if:
   115	
   116	- Every hypothesis is a **named intermediate fact** that also appears in the
   117	  paper or blueprint proof, not the theorem's output packaged up, and
   118	- Replacing a hypothesis with its negation would produce a *different*
   119	  theorem, not a trivially-false one.
   120	
   121	### Related issues and patterns
   122	
   123	- [#449] — paper-wide gap tracker
   124	- [#451] — the tracked `BridgePackage` producer catalogue
   125	- [#595] — resolved the QXP `ProjectiveNonMeasurementBridgePackage` offender by
   126	  deleting the bridge and threading `RoundingToProjectorsWitness` directly
   127	- [#477] — resolved `QXPLayerData` axiom-field projection (a definitional variant)
   128	- [#493] — the inline-existential mutation of this pattern
   129	- [#491] — PR that introduced the mutation
   130	
   131	---
   132	
   133	## A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand
   134	
   135	**Smell.** A `def`/`abbrev` is written so its body is the paper's claim, and
   136	a nearby `theorem` restates that claim and proves it by `rfl` (or a one-line
   137	`simp [foo]` where `foo` is the defining equation). The "mathematical
   138	content" has been baked into the definition; the theorem is a tautology. See
   139	issues [#477], [#494].
   140	
   141	### Why it's bad
   142	
   143	`rfl` proves that a definition equals itself. If the definition is chosen
   144	*so that* it equals the conclusion, the `rfl` "proof" transports none of the
   145	paper's reasoning — it is literally the reflexivity of a shape we invented to
   146	match the conclusion. The real identity the paper proves (e.g.,
   147	`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ` over an actual inner product) is still not stated
   148	anywhere in Lean.
   149	
   150	### How to spot it
   151	
   152	- A `theorem` whose body is `rfl` / `by rfl` / `by simp [defName]` where
   153	  `defName` is the def that unfolds to the conclusion.
   154	- A `structure` with a `Prop`-typed field whose *role* in the paper is a
   155	  nontrivial identity (SVD, orthonormality, Cauchy–Schwarz), accompanied by a
   156	  constructor that discharges that field with `rfl`.
   157	- A `def foo := if α = β then 1 else 0` followed by a theorem asserting
   158	  `foo α β = if α = β then 1 else 0`.
   159	- Bridge-like structures where every field is itself a function
   160	  `(precondition) → (conclusion-step)` and the consumer applies the field
   161	  directly.
   162	
   163	### Concrete example
   164	
   165	From `MIPStarRE/LDT/ExpansionHypercubeGraph/Defs/Fourier.lean`:
   166	
   167	```lean
   168	/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/
   169	def fourierBasisInnerProduct (params : Parameters)
   170	    (α β : Point params) : Error :=
